scenes.heading: Design a Real-time Analytics System
scenes.narration: Let us design a system that ingests high-velocity events and answers analytical queries within seconds, powering live dashboards and alerting on fresh data.

scenes.heading: Requirements and constraints
bullets: Ingest millions of events per second
Query latency in the low seconds
scenes.narration: The system must ingest millions of events per second without dropping data. It must answer analytical queries within a second or two so dashboards feel live. It needs windowed aggregations computed over event time, not arrival time, so results are correct. And it must gracefully handle late and out-of-order events, which are inevitable across distributed producers, using watermarks and grace periods.

scenes.heading: Real-time analytics flow
steps: Stream engine windows by event time
Materialize into a real-time OLAP store
scenes.narration: Events flow into a partitioned log like Kafka that buffers the high-velocity stream. A stream-processing engine consumes it and groups events into windows based on their event time. Watermarks track how far event time has progressed and decide when a window can be closed, tolerating a bounded amount of lateness. The engine materializes results into a real-time OLAP store such as Druid, Pinot, or ClickHouse. Dashboards then query that store and get answers in the low seconds even as data keeps arriving.

scenes.heading: Event time vs processing time

right.label: Processing time
points: When the system saw the event
Wrong results if data is delayed

scenes.narration: Event time is when the event actually happened at the source, and windowing on it produces correct aggregations even when events arrive late or out of order, at the cost of needing watermarks to know when to finalize a window. Processing time is simply when the system received the event, which is easy to implement and needs no watermarks, but it produces wrong results whenever the network or a backlog delays data. For trustworthy real-time analytics, window on event time and manage lateness with watermarks.

scenes.heading: Choosing the serving store
bullets: Ingests streams and answers in the low seconds
scenes.narration: The serving store is what makes queries feel instant. Real-time OLAP engines such as Druid, Apache Pinot, and ClickHouse are purpose-built for this role. They ingest streaming data continuously and answer analytical queries in the low seconds. They rely on columnar layouts and pre-aggregation to scan efficiently. And they support high query concurrency, so many dashboard users and alerting rules can hit the same fresh data at once without slowing each other down.

scenes.heading: Correctness under failure
bullets: Replay from the log on recovery
Idempotent writes to the OLAP store
scenes.narration: A real-time system must stay correct through failures. The stream processor checkpoints its windowed state periodically so it can recover without starting over. On recovery it replays events from the durable log to rebuild any lost progress. Exactly-once semantics ensure that replayed events are not counted twice. And writes to the serving store are made idempotent so that a retry after a crash produces the same result, keeping the numbers on the dashboard trustworthy even after an outage.

scenes.text: Buffer in a log, window on event time with watermarks, and serve from a real-time OLAP store for correct, fast live analytics.
scenes.narration: Buffer the firehose in a partitioned log, window on event time with watermarks to stay correct under lateness, and serve results from a purpose-built real-time OLAP store to get analytics that are both fast and trustworthy.
